question.question: An AI/ML engineer is building a Docker image for a PyTorch training workload that requires GPU access. The base image is nvidia/cuda:12.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04. Which of the following practices are recommended for this scenario?

options.text: Use a multi-stage build to separate the build environment (with compilers, CUDA toolkit) from the runtime environment (runtime-only CUDA libraries)
Install Python packages with pip using --no-cache-dir and combine all pip installs into a single RUN layer to minimize image size
Run the container with --privileged flag to ensure GPU access works correctly
Set the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable in the Dockerfile to restrict which GPUs the container can see
Use COPY --from=builder to copy only the installed packages from the build stage, excluding source code and build artifacts
Mount the host's /dev/nvidia0 directly into the container using -v /dev/nvidia0:/dev/nvidia0 for GPU access

question.explanation: A) Multi-stage builds are recommended to keep runtime images small by excluding build tools and CUDA toolkit. B) Combining pip installs into one RUN layer with --no-cache-dir reduces layer count and avoids caching pip's cache. E) COPY --from=builder correctly transfers only necessary artifacts. C) --privileged is a security risk; GPU access should use --gpus all (Docker 19.03+) or nvidia-container-toolkit. D) NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES should be set at runtime (docker run -e), not baked into the image, to allow flexibility. F) Direct device mounting is outdated; modern Docker uses --gpus flag with nvidia-container-runtime.
concepts_tested: GPU containerization with NVIDIA Container Toolkit
